title: Across the Water

pages.text:
*Jun's phone says: 58%, one bar. Nari's river says: fast in the middle, quiet at the edges.*

The water was not the same river they had looked at an hour ago. It was darker, broader, and it moved with a heavy, lazy force that made the small wooden hull of the Pear rock gently. Nari sat in the stern, her hands locked around the oars, her knuckles white. She pulled the boat away from the bank with a steady rhythm, dipping the blades into the current and drawing them back.

Jun sat in the bow, his knees pressed together. He held the flashlight, though he did not turn it on yet. In his other hand, he gripped the edge of the loose tarp. The rain was light, just a mist that smelled of wet earth and cold stone. He expected the far bank to be close. It looked close, just a strip of dark green grass and reeds across the water.

But the river was wide.

Nari did not look back. She did not check her phone. She simply watched the water, her eyes narrowed against the dim light. Jun wanted to tell her to be careful. He wanted to tell her that the current looked strong. Instead, he sat very still. He watched her hands. He watched the way the oars cut the water. For once, he did not say a single word.
pages.image: In a dark misty river at dusk, Nari in her sunflower-yellow T-shirt and orange life vest steers the green boat with an oar while Jun in his white T-shirt, round glasses and orange life vest sits in the bow holding a flashlight.

pages.text:
The far bank was soft mud, and Jun’s white sneakers sank into it with a squelch that he could feel in his teeth. The field was a sea of green stalks, and in the middle of it, the pepper plants stood in neat rows. The tarp was only half over them. Half of the red peppers were safe under the plastic. The other half were exposed to the rain, their bright skins glistening with water droplets.

They did not talk about who would do what. They just started.

Nari grabbed the heavy plastic sheet and pulled. Jun ran to the opposite side and grabbed it too. The tarp was slick and heavy. They pulled it taut, stretching it over the top of the pepper plants. Nari dropped to her knees in the mud, her dark green trousers instantly soaked to the knee. She began to look for stones.

Jun found a rock, then two. He placed them on the corner of the tarp. Nari followed. They worked in a blur of motion, shaking off rain, pulling plastic, weighing stones. It was faster than either of them expected. When the last corner was anchored, the peppers were safe, hidden under a shield of grey plastic. They stood up, breathing hard, and looked at each other. Neither smiled. Neither spoke.
pages.image: In a muddy field at night, Nari in her yellow shirt and orange life vest kneels securing a plastic tarp over red peppers with stones while Jun in his white T-shirt, orange life vest and white sneakers, wearing no hat, pulls the other side of the tarp taut.

pages.text:
The rain had stopped, but the air still felt thick and heavy. The Pear drifted a little away from the bank, bobbing in the gentle current. They had to tie it up. Nari took the thick rope from the bow and walked to the wooden post at the water's edge. She began to wrap the rope around the post, her movements quick and sure.

"Let me do it," Jun said.

Nari did not stop. "You don't know how."

"I saw a video," Jun said, pushing his glasses up his nose. "It's a bowline. It's stronger than a hitch. It won't slip."

Nari tied the knot she knew, the one Harabeoji had taught her a thousand times. It was a simple, tight wrap. Jun stepped forward and tried to take the rope from her hands. Nari pulled back. The rope stood between them, taut and waiting.

"Your grandfather does it this way," Jun said, trying to sound reasonable.

"Your internet does it that way," Nari said. "It's a boat, not a car. You need a knot that holds when it's wet."

"You need a knot that holds when it's fast," Jun countered. "We're going to be stuck out here if it slips."

Nari looked at him. She looked at the rope. She looked at the water, which was moving faster than it had an hour ago.
pages.image: Nari and Jun stand on a muddy riverbank at night, both wearing orange life vests, gripping a thick rope tied to a wooden post, looking at each other with stubborn expressions while the dark river flows behind them.

pages.text:
Nari let go of the rope. Jun took it. He began to tie the bowline, his fingers clumsy in the cold air. Nari watched him. She saw a mistake, a loop that was too loose. She reached out and adjusted it. Jun frowned. He tried to pull the loop tight, but Nari was already tying the second part of her hitch over his knot.

It was a mess. It looked like a pretzel that had been left in the rain. It was part bowline and part hitch, a tangled knot that belonged to neither of them. It was not beautiful. It was not efficient. But it was thick, and it was tight, and it was holding.

Jun stepped back. "It's fine," he said.

Nari wiped her hands on her trousers. "It's fine," she agreed.

They both looked at the knot. It squatted at the base of the post, looking slightly offended. Neither of them said it was strong. Neither of them said it was weak. They just looked at the boat, which was now securely tied, and the dark water that lapped at the hull. The rain had started again, a soft, steady drizzle that turned the air into a cool mist.
pages.image: Jun and Nari, both in orange life vests, look down at a complex, tangled rope knot tied around a wooden post on a muddy riverbank, with the small wooden boat visible in the dark water behind them.

pages.text:
The last corner of the tarp remained loose, slapping wet against the pepper plants. Jun grabbed one edge of the plastic while Nari took the other, and they hauled it tight together. They pressed down on the final stone, anchoring the sheet.

Then the wind changed.

It no longer blew from the north or the south. Instead, it rushed down from upstream, carrying a chill that smelled of deep water and mud. Nari stopped pulling. She stood very still, sniffing the air and squinting up the valley where the hills disappeared into the dark sky.

A sound came down the river. It was not a crash or a roar. It was a long, low hush, rolling over the water, the field, and the two of them.

Nari turned to Jun. Her face was pale in the dim light.

"Jun," she said. "Look at the river."
pages.image: Nari, a sunburnt girl in an orange vest, squints upstream toward the dark hills while Jun, a thin boy in glasses and an orange vest, looks at her with wide eyes, both standing in a muddy field with a plastic tarp over red peppers.
